PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.title: Two Sum Target Pairs
PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target. You may assume that each input has exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice.

starterCode.sql:
-- Relational pair matching
SELECT a.id AS idx1, b.id AS idx2
FROM numbers a
JOIN numbers b ON a.id < b.id
WHERE a.val + b.val = 9;

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.hint: A brute force O(N^2) double loop works, but an O(N) hash map storing { value: index } provides optimal linear time lookup.

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.title: Top Revenue Generating Customers (SQL)
PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.description: Write an SQL query to retrieve the top 5 customers by total order spend in the current fiscal year. Only include customers who placed at least 3 distinct orders and spent more than ₹50,000 total. Output customer_id, customer_name, total_orders, and total_spend.

examples.input:
Table: orders (order_id, customer_id, amount, order_date)
Table: customers (customer_id, name)
examples.output:
customer_id | customer_name | total_orders | total_spend
101 | Rajesh Kumar | 5 | 84,500
204 | Priya Sharma | 4 | 67,200
examples.explanation: Filters on COUNT(order_id) >= 3 and SUM(amount) > 50000 ordered by total_spend descending.

starterCode.sql:
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.name AS customer_name,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders,
    SUM(o.amount) AS total_spend
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) >= 3 AND SUM(o.amount) > 50000
ORDER BY total_spend DESC
LIMIT 5;

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.hint: Remember to apply the aggregate conditions in the HAVING clause rather than the WHERE clause.

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.title: Implement Custom Debounce Function
PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.description: Implement a debounce function that takes a callback function fn and a delay in milliseconds t. The returned function should delay the execution of fn until t milliseconds have elapsed since the last time the debounced function was invoked.

examples.explanation: The call at t=0ms was cancelled because another call arrived at t=50ms before the 100ms timer elapsed.

starterCode.python:
import time
import threading

def debounce(fn, wait_seconds):
    timer = None
    def debounced(*args, **kwargs):
        nonlocal timer
        if timer:
            timer.cancel()
        timer = threading.Timer(wait_seconds, lambda: fn(*args, **kwargs))
        timer.start()
    return debounced

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.hint: Use a closure to hold the active timer ID. Whenever the returned function is called, immediately clear the previous timer.

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.title: Find the Missing Number in Consecutive Sequence
PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.description: Given an array nums containing n distinct numbers in the range [0, n], return the only number in the range that is missing from the array. Aim for O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

examples.explanation: n = 3 since there are 3 numbers, so all numbers are in [0,3]. 2 is missing.

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.hint: Calculate the mathematical sum from 0 to n using n*(n+1)/2 and subtract the array sum to get the missing element in O(1) space.

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.title: Department Salary Ranking with Window Functions
PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.description: Write an SQL query to find the top 3 highest-earning employees in each department. If employees have identical salaries, they should share the same rank without skipping rank numbers.

examples.input:
Table: Employee (id, name, salary, department_id)
Table: Department (id, name)
examples.output:
department_name | employee_name | salary | rank
Engineering | Amit Verma | 185000 | 1
Engineering | Sneha Rao | 165000 | 2
examples.explanation: Uses DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) <= 3.

starterCode.sql:
WITH RankedSalaries AS (
    SELECT 
        d.name AS department_name,
        e.name AS employee_name,
        e.salary,
        DENSE_RANK() OVER (
            PARTITION BY e.department_id 
            ORDER BY e.salary DESC
        ) AS salary_rank
    FROM Employee e
    JOIN Department d ON e.department_id = d.id
)
SELECT department_name, employee_name, salary, salary_rank
FROM RankedSalaries
WHERE salary_rank <= 3
ORDER BY department_name, salary_rank;

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.hint: Use DENSE_RANK() instead of RANK() so that tied salaries do not create gaps in the rank sequence.

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.title: Merge Overlapping Intervals
PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.description: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], merge all overlapping intervals, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input.

examples.explanation: Since intervals [1,3] and [2,6] overlap, merge them into [1,6].

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.hint: Sort the intervals by their start time first. Once sorted, a consecutive interval can only overlap with the preceding merged interval.

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.title: SQL Running Total / Cumulative Sum
PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.description: Write an SQL query to calculate the daily total transaction amount along with a cumulative running total across all days. Output transaction_date, daily_total, and running_cumulative_total.

examples.explanation: Uses SUM(daily_total) OVER (ORDER BY transaction_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).

starterCode.sql:
WITH DailyTotals AS (
    SELECT 
        transaction_date,
        SUM(amount) AS daily_total
    FROM Transactions
    GROUP BY transaction_date
)
SELECT 
    transaction_date,
    daily_total,
    SUM(daily_total) OVER (
        ORDER BY transaction_date 
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS running_cumulative_total
FROM DailyTotals
ORDER BY transaction_date;

testCases.expected: Cumulative total accurately accumulates each day

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.hint: First aggregate amounts per day using a CTE, then apply a window SUM with ORDER BY transaction_date.

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.title: LRU Cache Eviction Architecture
PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.description: Design a data structure that follows the constraints of a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache with get(key) and put(key, value) operations executing in O(1) average time complexity.

examples.explanation: Key 1 was accessed before put(3), making key 2 the least recently used element.

PRACTICE_QUESTIONS.hint: A Doubly Linked List paired with a Hash Map offers O(1) removals and insertions at both head and tail.
